transcript.text: There's water all over the kitchen floor coming from under my Beko washing machine and its gone under the units to where the plug is, the machine is still going. What do I do?

Don't touch the plug, the socket, or the machine while there's water around them. Water and mains electricity together can give you a serious shock.

## Do this now

1. Turn off the power at the fuse box (consumer unit).
• Make sure you're standing somewhere dry, with dry hands.
• Switch off the circuit for the kitchen sockets. If you're not sure which one, flip the main switch to cut power to the whole house.
• If you can't reach the fuse box without walking through water, or it's sparking, smoking, or buzzing, leave it, get everyone out of the kitchen, and call an electrician.

2. Turn off the water to the machine.
• Once the power is off, find the isolation valve on the pipe behind or beside the machine (often under the sink) and turn it so the lever is across the pipe.
• If you can't find it, turn off your main stopcock (usually under the kitchen sink).

3. Keep children and pets out of the kitchen.

## Once it's safe

• Mop up the water with towels, a mop, or a wet vac. Get under the units as well as you can.
• Unplug the machine, but only once the power is off and the socket area is completely dry.
• Don't use that socket again until it's thoroughly dried out. If water got into it, have an electrician check it before you switch it back on.
• Drain the machine before moving it. Beko machines have a small filter flap at the bottom front. Put towels and a shallow tray down first, because a lot of water can come out.

## Likely causes (to check later)

• A loose or split inlet or drain hose at the back
• A blocked filter (often coins, hair grips, or fluff)
• The drain hose popped out of the standpipe or sink waste
• A damaged door seal
• Too much detergent causing overflow

If it's not an obvious hose or filter problem, contact Beko or a repair engineer, especially if the machine is still under warranty.

Are you able to get to your fuse box safely? If you tell me what you're seeing, I can help with the next step.
yes the fuse box is in the hall and the floor's dry there. I'm standing in the kitchen in my socks though and the floor is soaking, should I get out first? the machine is still running

Yes, get out of the kitchen first. Ignore the machine for now. It running for another minute is fine.

1. Walk out carefully toward the hall. Wet socks on a wet floor are slippery, so go slowly.
2. Don't touch anything on the way out: not the washing machine, other appliances, the sink, taps, radiators, or metal handles. Keep your hands to yourself.
3. Once you're on the dry hall floor, take off the wet socks and dry your hands and feet thoroughly.
4. Then switch off at the fuse box. If you're not sure which switch is the kitchen sockets, just flip the main switch to turn off the whole house. Use your phone torch if it gets dark.

If at any point you feel tingling, see sparks, smell burning, or the fuse box looks scorched, don't touch it. Stay out of the kitchen and call an electrician (or 999 if there's fire or someone is hurt).

Let me know once the power's off and I'll walk you through shutting off the water and draining the machine.
ok I'm out in the hall now, floor's dry. I took my socks off and dried my hands. Switching the power off at the fuse box now, ok?

Yes, go ahead.

At the fuse box:
• Use one hand and touch only the switch.
• Flip the main switch (usually the biggest one, often red or labelled "Main Switch") to OFF. That's the quickest and safest way to be sure the kitchen is dead.
• If it trips back or won't stay off, or you see sparks or scorching, step away and call an electrician.

Check it worked:
• The washing machine should go quiet, and lights in the house should go off.
• If the machine is still running, the power isn't fully off. Don't go back in. Let me know.

Once it's off:
1. Put on dry shoes or wellies before going back into the kitchen.
2. Turn off the water. Find the isolation valve on the pipe behind or beside the machine, or under the sink, and turn it so the lever is across the pipe. If you can't find it, use the main stopcock, usually under the sink.
3. Start mopping up, especially around the socket and under the units.

Don't open the washing machine door yet. There may be a lot of water inside. Tell me when the power and water are off and I'll talk you through draining it.
ok it's off, the machine has gone quiet. I'm putting shoes on now. the water has definitely run back towards the socket, the floor under the plug is wet. is that ok to mop?

Yes, it's safe to mop now. With the main switch off and the machine quiet, there's no power at that socket.

While you mop:
• Turn the water off first if you haven't yet (isolation valve or stopcock), so no more comes out.
• Mop or towel up the water around and under the plug. Soak it up rather than splashing.
• Leave the plug and socket alone for now. Don't unplug or wipe inside the socket.
• Get as far under the units as you can. Towels pushed under with a broom handle work well.

Before turning the power back on:
• Leave the main switch off until the floor under the socket is dry and the socket itself looks dry.
• If water reached the socket itself (wet faceplate, water dripping onto it, or water pooled around the back), leave it off and get an electrician to check it before using it again.
• If you need lights or the fridge back on sooner, an electrician can help you isolate just the kitchen sockets. Or, if your fuse box is clearly labelled, you could switch the main back on with only the kitchen sockets circuit left off. But if in doubt, keep it all off.
• Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. They'll stay cold for several hours.

Let me know once the floor's mopped and the water's off, and I'll talk you through draining the machine safely.
ok thanks, mopping now. I'm not sure if the water got inside the socket itself, how would I tell? the machine's still full of water too, I can't pull it out on my own, it's really heavy

## Checking the socket

Keep the power off while you look. Use your phone torch and look only, don't touch or poke inside it.

Signs water may have got in:
• Water or droplets on the faceplate, or around the edges where it meets the wall or unit
• Damp or dark patches on the wall or panel around or below it
• The socket sitting at or near floor level where the water was pooling
• Water dripping from above it, or the plug itself looking wet
• Any scorch marks or a burning smell

Probably fine if the socket is clearly mounted above where the water reached and it and the wall around it look completely dry.

If you're not sure, treat it as wet. Leave the kitchen sockets off and get an electrician to check it before using it. If your fuse box is labelled, you can switch the main back on with just the kitchen sockets circuit off, so you get your lights and other rooms back. If anything trips when you do that, switch it off and leave it for the electrician.

## Draining the machine (don't try to pull it out full)

You can drain it from the front where it is, with the power still off:

1. Find the flap at the bottom front corner of the machine. Prise it open with a coin or flat screwdriver.
2. Lay towels down and get a shallow container (a baking tray or roasting tin works). There could be several litres, so expect to empty it a few times.
3. If there's a small black hose behind the flap, pull it out, point it into the tray and remove its cap. Let it drain, put the cap back on when the tray's nearly full, empty it, and repeat.
4. If there's no hose, slowly unscrew the round filter anticlockwise just a little and let water trickle out. Tighten it to stop the flow while you empty the tray. Once it's fully drained, take the filter out and check it for coins, hair grips or fluff. Rinse it and screw it back in firmly.
5. Once it stops draining, you can open the door and take the washing out. It'll be wet, so have a bucket or basket ready.

An empty machine is much lighter, but it's still worth having someone help you pull it out to look at the hoses.

Did the socket look dry or wet when you checked?

I can't really tell, the socket is under the worktop behind the machine so I can't see it properly. I know the floor under the plug was wet though. I'll leave it off, but should I start draining the machine now?

Yes, start draining now. With the main switch off it's safe, and leaving the kitchen sockets off until an electrician checks them is the right call.

## Before you start
• Make sure the water supply is off (isolation valve or stopcock), if you haven't done it yet.
• Check the temperature. If it was on a hot wash, feel the door glass. If it's hot, wait 20-30 minutes for it to cool so you don't get scalded.
• Put down plenty of towels and get a shallow tray or roasting tin, plus a bucket to empty it into.

## Draining
1. Open the flap at the bottom front corner with a coin or flat screwdriver.
2. If there's a small black hose behind the flap, pull it out, hold the end in the tray and remove the cap. Cap it again when the tray's nearly full, empty it into the bucket, and repeat.
3. If there's no hose, unscrew the round filter anticlockwise just a little so water trickles out. Tighten it to stop the flow each time you empty the tray.
4. Be patient. There may be 10 litres or more, so expect lots of trips.
5. When it stops, remove the filter completely and check for coins, hair grips or fluff. A blockage here is a common cause of leaks. Rinse it and screw it back in firmly.
6. Open the door and take the washing out into a basket or bucket.

## Afterwards
• Once it's empty, you should be able to ease the machine forward, rocking it side to side. With the power still off, you can unplug it and look at the socket and the hoses at the back. You may spot a loose or split hose.
• Dry the floor behind it properly and leave the area open to air out.
• Don't use the machine again until you've found the cause of the leak.

Your fuse box may have labelled switches. If it does, you can switch the main back on with just the kitchen sockets circuit left off, so you get lights and the fridge back. If anything trips, switch it off and leave it for the electrician.

Let me know how the draining goes or what you find behind the machine.
ok starting to drain it now, I've got towels down and a baking tray. will let you know what I find

Good luck. A few quick tips while you go:

• Go slowly with the filter. If it gushes, tighten it a bit. A small trickle is easier to manage.
• Don't overfill the tray. Baking trays spill easily when you lift them. Empty it when it's about half full.
• Expect it to take a while. Draining through the filter can take 15-30 minutes or more.
• If the filter won't budge, don't force it with tools. Wrap a towel round it for grip. If it still won't turn, leave it and we'll look at other options.
• If the flow stops but the drum is clearly still full, the filter or hose may be blocked with fluff. Gently clear the opening.

I'm here when you're done. Let me know what you find in the filter or behind the machine.
